Robin opened his shirt to reveal a small bag hanging around his neck. "I'm hiding this from Robin Hood."

The merchant's eyes widened as Robin showed him some gold coins. "Put that money away, you fool!" said the merchant. "If Robin Hood catches you, he'll take everything you have. He hates dishonest beggars as much as greedy merchants."
"Oh, I had no idea!" Robin pretended to be surprised. "May I walk with you? We seem to be going in the same direction."
"Well, all right," said the corn merchant. "I don't mind your company, now that I know you're an honest man."

The two men traveled in silence until they reached the outskirts of Sherwood Forest. Then the merchant turned to Robin. "We're getting close to where Robin Hood lives. Here's where you're in the greatest danger, my friend."
"I wish I had as little money with me as you do," said Robin. "I'm afraid Robin Hood will steal my gold."
The merchant laughed and winked at Robin. "I'll tell you a secret. I have more money with me than you do. But it's hidden in a place Robin Hood will never find."
Robin opened his eyes wide. "Really?"
The merchant nodded. "See my shoes? The soles of my clogs are actually boxes. I've hidden ninety pounds in gold coins in each one."
"In the soles of your clogs?" Robin laughed until he cried.
The merchant stared at Robin with a frown. "There's nothing to laugh at!"
But Robin was still chuckling. "I really like those clogs. Take them off and give them to me. If you don't take them off, I'll summon my friends."
The merchant turned pale. "Who are you really?"
"Everyone calls me Robin Hood!"
The merchant shook with fear as he removed his clogs. Robin made him open the soles and count out the coins.
"Now get out of here!" Robin said sternly. "I've heard many stories about how you've cheated the poor. If I hear any more of these stories, you'll be in real trouble!"
The merchant rode away as fast as he could.

That night in Sherwood Forest the fire stayed lit for a long time. Around the glowing fire, Robin and Little John entertained the men with stories of their adventures as a beggar and a friar. The men listened closely, laughing at their tales.
When they were finished, Friar Tuck spoke up. "I still believe that the life of the friar is happier than the life of the beggar."
Will Scarlet shook his head. "I think Robin's day was more fun. He tricked those beggars and that nasty corn merchant."
The other men quickly put in their opinions, arguing loudly. Some agreed with Friar Tuck, and others agreed with Will.
But Robin and Little John just laughed. They'd both had entertaining adventures!

Little John and Will Scarlet were sitting outside the Blue Boar Inn. A young man arrived on a beautiful white horse. The man was dressed in silk and velvet clothing, which was trimmed with gold and jewels.
He hurried toward Little John and Will. "Do you know where I can find Robin Hood?" he asked.
"What do you want with him?" Will demanded. He was suspicious of any stranger asking about Robin.
"I have a message from Queen Eleanor," the young man said. "It's important. I'm her page."
Will and Little John looked at each other, unsure of what to do.
Little John shrugged. "This page seems harmless," he said. "I think we can take him to Robin."
Will nodded, and soon the two men were guiding the page through Sherwood Forest.
Robin was sitting under a tree with several of his men. Alan of Dale was playing his harp and singing.
Robin got to his feet when he saw the men coming. He was surprised to see the finely dressed page deep in the woods.
"Tell me, what brings you to Sherwood Forest?" asked Robin.

The page climbed down from his horse and bowed to Robin. "I bring greetings from Queen Eleanor," he said. "King Henry is holding a very large shooting match in London in four days. All the best archers in England will be there. Queen Eleanor would like you and some of your men to compete."
"I'm honored." Robin bowed his head.
"The queen promises to protect you and send you safely home." The page held out a gold ring. "She gives you this ring as a sign of her promise."
Robin placed the ring on his little finger. "Get ready, Will and Little John! We're going to London!"
After several days of travel, the three men arrived at the palace. Queen Eleanor looked happy to see them. She greeted them with a smile and made sure they had plenty to eat.
"I've heard so much about you," she said. "But I'd like to hear more. Tell me about your adventures."
So Robin and his men told her many tales. She especially liked the story about the Bishop of Hereford and the feast.
"We made him stay with us in Sherwood Forest for three days!" said Little John.
The queen laughed at that. "I hope you're as good at archery as you are at telling stories!" She lowered her voice and explained her plan.

The next morning was bright and sunny. Hundreds of archers gathered on a large field, ready to compete. King Henry and Queen Eleanor sat on thrones trimmed in silver and gold. A trumpet sounded, and the archers lined up in neat rows.
Robin, Little John, and Will Scarlet hid themselves among the people watching. Instead of their usual green clothes, the three men wore blue to disguise themselves.
"Queen Eleanor will tell us when it's time to appear," said Robin. "For now let's enjoy the shooting match."
In the first round, each archer shot seven arrows.
"Wow!" exclaimed Will. "This is the biggest shooting match I've ever been to!"
It took a long time to get through that first round. And then there were several more rounds. As the day wore on, more archers were eliminated. At last only three men remained.
Queen Eleanor turned to King Henry. "Do you think those are the best archers in England?"
The king gazed at the archers proudly. "Those men are from my guard," said the king. "They're the best in the world!"
"Well, I know three men who are better archers," said the queen.
The king laughed. "What do you know about archery?"

The queen smiled. "You might be surprised by my knowledge. The three men will enter the contest, but you must promise not to harm them. After the contest you must allow them to travel freely for forty days."
King Henry looked puzzled. "Those are strange conditions, but I promise."
The queen motioned for her page. She whispered in his ear, "Tell Robin and his men it's time for their match."
"My dear," said the king. "You have such an interest in archery now. Shall we bet on this match? I'll bet two hundred fine bows and arrows."
"I'll bet this beautiful belt." The queen pointed to her waist. "Its jewels are worth far more than your bows and arrows."
People began whispering, wondering what the queen was up to. One thing was certain: this promised to be an interesting match!
It was the final round of King Henry's archery contest. The Bishop of Hereford sat next to the queen.
The king's page led three men onto the field. They were named Gilbert, Tepus, and Hubert. They bowed to the king and queen.

The queen's page led three men onto the field. They were Robin Hood, Little John, and Will Scarlet. When the queen's archers bowed, the Bishop of Hereford looked startled, as if he'd just been stung by a wasp.
"I know those men!" he shouted in surprise. "They're—"
"Robert of Locksley and his friends," the queen said with a smile. Robin used this name when he was in disguise.
The bishop's face was red with anger, but he didn't say anything more.
"Locksley!" the queen called to Robin. "I've made a bet with the king. I told him that you and your men can outshoot any of his men. I hope, for my sake, that I'm not wrong."
"We'll do our best for you!" said Robin.
Little John shifted his feet, looking a little shy. "You're so lovely, Queen Eleanor," he said. "Is there anyone who wouldn't do their best for you?"
The queen laughed. But the bishop didn't crack a smile. And neither did King Henry. He was glaring at his wife.
"Who are these men?" the king demanded.
Before the queen could speak, the bishop leaped to his feet.

"Locksley is really the outlaw Robin Hood!" he burst out. "That giant fellow is called Little John, and the other one is Will Scarlet. They both belong to Robin Hood's band. All three of them are robbers and thieves."
The king looked stunned. "Is this true?" he asked the queen sternly.

"Yes," the queen replied, smiling. "The bishop knows these men well. He and some of his friars spent three days with them in Sherwood Forest. Remember, dear, you promised these archers would be safe for forty days."

"I'll keep my promise." The king scowled. "But when those forty days are up, Robin Hood should beware. Things may not go exactly as he wants." He turned to Gilbert, Tepus, and Hubert. "If you beat Robin Hood and his men, I'll reward you well. Go now, and do your best."
The men began to get ready, stringing their bows and carefully selecting their arrows.

The match began. No one had ever seen such amazing shooting. Hubert went first, and made his best shots of the day. Will Scarlet went next. He shot too cautiously and couldn't beat Hubert. Little John easily beat Tepus. Gilbert tried his best and hit two bull's-eyes with his three arrows.
"Well done, Gilbert!" Robin slapped him on the shoulder. "You really should come to Sherwood Forest." He picked up his bow, selected an arrow, and then instantly shot a bull's-eye.
The crowd gasped.
"There's nothing interesting to shoot here in London," Robin said to Gilbert. He shot another bull's-eye.
"What do you think?" Robin hit another bull's-eye.
A murmur went through the crowd and then everyone started clapping.
Gilbert rushed to shake hands with Robin. "I think you're the best archer in the world!"
King Henry wasn't so gracious. "It's time for us to go," he snapped at Queen Eleanor. They stood up and left the field, without watching the judges give Robin first prize.
Robin won a trumpet, a purse of gold coins, and ten gold arrows.
"I'll keep this silver trumpet," said Robin after the ceremony. "But, Gilbert, you shot the best of the king's men. So I am giving you the purse of gold coins."
At this, the crowd cheered.
"What will you do with the ten gold arrows?" asked Little John.
"I'll give them to the top ten archers," replied Robin.
Another loud cheer rose from the crowd.
Robin handed out the arrows to the men. "Keep them to remember this day. It was an honor to compete against you."
"Hooray!" cried the crowd. "Hooray for Robin!"
The archers swarmed around Robin and his men, eager to meet them. Everyone was talking loudly. A member of the king's guard tapped Robin's shoulder.
"I have a message for you," said the guard. "The queen's page said to tell you: The lion growls. Beware. Do you know what that means?"
"Yes." Robin nodded. "Thank you for delivering this warning." He turned to his men. "Little John! Will! We must be going."
As they hurried away, Robin explained the reason for their haste.
"That was a message from the queen," he said. "King Henry is furious!"
King Henry was extremely angry. He'd promised Queen Eleanor that her three archers could go free for forty days. But the archers turned out to be Robin Hood and his men!
When the king returned to his castle, he sat in silence, furiously biting his lip. The Bishop of Hereford sat with him. So did a good, honest knight named Sir Lee.

Finally the bishop spoke up. "Your Majesty, I know you want to keep your promise to the queen. But Robin Hood is right here in London. He's the greatest villain in England. It's a shame to let him get away."
The king lifted his eyes and looked glumly at the bishop. "I can't break my word to my wife. When forty days have passed, we'll go after Robin Hood."

The Bishop of Hereford hated Robin and his men. He spoke carefully, in a soft, smooth voice. "Once Robin returns to Sherwood Forest, you'll never find him, Your Majesty. He knows that area far better than you do."
The king tapped his fingers on the table in front of him. "But what about my promise? Didn't you hear me give her my word?"

The bishop cleared his throat. "You of course know your wife best, Your Majesty. But I'm sure that the queen has forgotten all about Robin Hood by now." He laughed loudly. "Women are so easily distracted."
The king thought about that. Then he finally made up his mind. "Sir Lee! Take six men and seize Robin at the archery field. Throw him and his two men in prison!"
Sir Lee was a gentle and noble knight. He was upset to hear the king breaking his word to his wife. But he couldn't say anything; he was only the king's servant.
"Yes, Your Majesty," Sir Lee mumbled. He bowed to the king and left the room.
Sir Lee had made up his mind about something too. Before rounding up the men, he found the queen and told her what had happened.
"You must warn Robin!" he said.
"Why are you so worried about an outlaw?" asked Queen Eleanor.
"I don't care about Robin," Sir Lee explained. "I'm upset that the king is breaking his promise to you!"
"I've already warned Robin that the king is angry," said the queen. "But now I must send another warning. Thank you, Sir Lee."
Meanwhile Robin and his men had already left London. It was almost dark when Robin pointed to an inn. "There's a place we can spend the night."
"And get something to eat," said Little John, who was always hungry.
Will Scarlet looked around uneasily. "I wish we were farther away from London," he murmured. "I'm sure the king will send men after us."
"Don't worry. We'll be safe here," said Robin.
Will still looked uneasy but he shrugged. "Whatever you say, Robin."
The three men went into the inn. The innkeeper served them a fine meal. Then, while they were busy eating, he approached Robin again.
"There's a young man outside who wants to speak to you," said the innkeeper. "He says he's the queen's page."
Robin got up from the table and went outside. Little John and Will looked at each other nervously.
Outside, the queen's page sat on his horse in the white moonlight.

"The queen sent me to warn you," said the page. "The Bishop of Hereford has encouraged the king to break his promise. King Henry sent Sir Lee to arrest you at the archery field. But you'd already left. More than a thousand men are after you right now!"
"This is the second time the queen has saved me," said Robin. "Please thank her for this new warning."
"Hurry!" the page urged him. "Two bands of horsemen are right behind me!"
"I'll tell the innkeeper we're going to Saint Albans," said Robin quickly. "But we won't go anywhere near that town."
Robin went inside and spoke to the innkeeper. "We won't be spending the night after all. We're heading to Saint Albans. Let's go, men!"
Back on the road, Robin explained what was happening.
"We should split up," said Will Scarlet. "I'll go with Little John, and you travel alone, Robin."
"We'll head in different directions," said Robin. "If we're caught, we won't be caught together."
"Right!" said Will. "See you at home!"
After eight days Will and Little John reached Sherwood Forest. Everyone rejoiced to see them.
"Sorry it took us so long," said Little John. "Where's Robin?"
"Robin?" said one of the men. "We thought he was with you."
The king's men hurried to Saint Albans, but Robin wasn't there. The Bishop of Hereford soon joined the king's men.
"The king put me in charge," announced the bishop.
He divided the men into small groups. They searched the countryside for Robin. They blocked every road and path. But there was no sign of Robin.
Then the Sheriff of Nottingham and all his men joined the bishop. "I look forward to capturing Robin," said the sheriff.
"So do I!" said the bishop.
Meanwhile Robin had been walking for days. He whistled as he walked along the road, unworried. Then he paused at a stream to wash his face and get a drink of water.
Suddenly something whizzed past his ear!
"An arrow!" cried Robin. He sprang to his feet and raced through the stream and into the dense woods.

The king's men galloped after him until they reached the woods. Then they left their horses and ran after him. But Robin knew the area much better than the king's men did. He crawled along the ground, and then stooped and ran, until finally he escaped the men.
Panting, he finally stopped at the top of a hill. Below he saw even more of the king's men.
"I need a disguise!" Robin's stomach growled. "And some food!"
Robin was careful to stay hidden as he walked toward Nottingham. He soon spotted a shoemaker.
"Hello, there!" Robin called. "I was admiring your outfit. Will you change clothes with me? And share your lunch?"
The shoemaker laughed. "Your clothes are much nicer than mine. Why do you want to change?"
"I'm playing a joke on someone." Robin held out his hand. "Here, I'll give you ten gold coins."
"All right!"
The two men changed clothes and sat down to eat. They were exchanging stories when the king's men suddenly interrupted them.
"There he is!" one of the men called.
"Robin Hood, you're under arrest!" said another man to the shoemaker.
"I'm not Robin Hood!" said the shoemaker.

But the king's men didn't listen to the shoemaker. They tied his hands behind him and then took him away. Robin knew the shoemaker would be all right. The bishop would quickly realize the shoemaker wasn't Robin.
So Robin continued walking. But by dark, he was exhausted.
"I'd better get some sleep," Robin thought. He stopped at the next inn along the road and got one of the last available beds. He fell asleep almost before his head touched the pillow.
When Robin awoke at dawn, he found a friar sleeping in the next bed.
Quickly he dressed in the friar's clothes. Outside he took the friar's mule and hurried away. Disguised as a friar, Robin passed right by some of the king's men.
As Robin rode down a lane, he spotted a familiar knight.
"Sir Richard, how nice to see you!" exclaimed Robin, leaping off the mule. "I've been on the run." He told Sir Richard about the men chasing him. "But I'll soon be safely back in Sherwood Forest."
Sir Richard shook his head. "You're in great danger, Robin. Everyone knows you're disguised as a friar. There's only one thing to do. Go back to London and ask for Queen Eleanor's help."
"Back to London?" Robin felt his heart sink.
"Yes, come with me," Sir Richard said. "You can dress as one of my men. We'll travel with you to London."
Robin didn't want to go back to London, but Sir Richard was a very wise knight. So Robin changed his clothes once again and followed Sir Richard.
Queen Eleanor was walking in her garden among the roses when a man leaped over the wall. He hung onto the wall for a moment before dropping lightly on the grass.
Her maids shrieked, but the queen recognized Robin.
"Your Majesty!" Robin knelt at her feet. "Help! The king's men are after me."
"What?" The queen looked furious. "The king has broken his promise. He won't get away with this! Wait here, Robin."

Queen Eleanor returned soon. "You can travel safely, Robin. The king has promised me again that you will be safe." Robin saw that her eyes were still bright with anger. "And this time he will not break his promise!"
After three days Robin set off for home again. Along the way he passed many of the king's men, but this time no one dared to harm him.
At last Robin arrived safely back in Sherwood Forest. And there he stayed for many years with his merry men, singing, feasting, and shooting his bow and arrow.
